headlines.title: Santa Rosa puts sales tax hike on November ballot
headlines.description: Santa Rosa voters will decide in November whether to extend and increase the city’s existing local sales tax to help fund public safety, road repairs and other city services as officials work to address ongoing budget shortfalls. The Santa Rosa City Council voted Tuesday to place the measure on the November 2026 ballot. If approved, it would reauthorize the city’s existing half-cent Measure Q sales tax at an updated 1-cent rate until ended by voters. City officials said the money would help support general services such as 911 emergency medical and fire response, police response to violent crimes, street and pothole repairs, and keeping public spaces safe and clean. City leaders said Santa Rosa has cut about $25 million in ongoing expenses over the past three fiscal years, including eliminating 82 positions, and has implemented pension reforms to help reduce a long-running structural budget deficit. If voters approve the measure, it is expected to generate about $46 million a year for city services. Mayor Mark Stapp said the city has already reduced spending on fire, police, street maintenance and other services because of budget pressures. He warned that without more local funding, more cuts are expected, including the planned rotating closure of fire stations that could slow emergency response times. Over 2,400 residents participated in a bilingual community outreach effort, with public safety and road maintenance emerging as the community’s top priorities, city officials said. A recent survey also found that up to 62% of respondents said they would support the tax measure. If approved, the measure would include independent audits and public disclosure of spending, according to city officials.

headlines.title: Crews stop forward progress of Ragione Fire in San Jose
headlines.description: Firefighters responded to a vegetation fire Wednesday afternoon in San Jose that burned between 0.5 and 1 acre, according to the San Jose Police Department. The fire, now known as the Ragione Fire, was reported near La Ragione Avenue and Albanese Circle. Officials said the fire spread at a slow rate. Traffic was impacted in the area as crews responded, and officials urged the public to avoid the area. SJPD said forward progress on the fire was stopped at 2 p.m.

headlines.title: ‘Terrified' dog spent 2 days in Caltrain tunnel in San Francisco before being rescued
headlines.description: A runaway dog spent two days in a dark Caltrain tunnel in San Francisco before he was rescued, San Francisco Animal Care and Control said Tuesday. On the first day, train operators saw the dog, later identified as Roo, and assumed it was a dead animal. However, on the second day, a train operator saw Roo move, according to Animal Care and Control. “He was so still they thought he had been hit by a train and was injured,” Animal Care and Control said in a post on social media. Animal Care and Control officers went into the tunnel with Caltrain staff and found Roo “scared” and “terrified” but not injured. “He was terrified at first then was thrilled to be rescued,” Animal Care and Control said. Roo was microchipped and safely reunited with his owner, who had been looking for him. Animal Care and Control said Roo was recently adopted and took off after getting spooked. View this post on Instagram A post shared by SF Animal Care & Control (@sfanimalcareandcontrol)

headlines.title: San Rafael gas leak: Crews stop line rupture, shelter-in-place order lifted
headlines.description: A gas leak in downtown San Rafael Wednesday morning triggered evacuations, a shelter-in-place order and road closures. Police said an accidental gas line rupture happened in the area of Fifth Avenue and B Street. People at Westamerica Bank, located at 1108 Fifth Ave., were instructed to evacuate to the north toward Mission Avenue or A Street. People at 1210 Fifth Ave. were instructed to evacuate toward Mission Avenue or C Street. A shelter-in-place order was issued for Fifth Avenue between A and C streets as well as B Street between Fourth Street and Mission Avenue. People in buildings were instructed to stay inside, turn off outside ventilation, and close and secure all windows and doors until the order is lifted. Police officers, firefighters and PG&E crews responded and worked to turn off the gas where the rupture occurred, police said. Authorities said by 12:30 p.m. crews had stopped the rupture and the shelter-in-place order was lifted. The following road closures were in place: Fifth Avenue between A Street and C Street B Street from Fourth Avenue to Mission Avenue Misson Avenue between Wilkins Street and C Street This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates.

headlines.title: Unpaid rent puts Oakland Roots' Coliseum match in jeopardy
headlines.description: The Oakland Roots are at risk of not being able to play Saturday’s match at the Coliseum after falling behind on rent payments to Alameda County and the city of Oakland. The authority that governs the Coliseum notified the team that it is in default on $1.381 million in past-due payments. The Roots presented a payment plan last Friday, but the board determined it was not acceptable. The board said the team must either pay the full amount owed or pay $173,000 per game, which includes a flat fee, a food and beverage deposit, facilities fees and parking. The team must also pay an additional $200,000 over the next six games toward the past-due balance. That per-game payment is due by noon Wednesday if the Roots want to play Saturday’s match at the Coliseum. The team has struggled with low attendance and has been operating at a loss. NBC Bay Area reached out to the Roots and the city of Oakland for comment but had not received a response Wednesday morning. The office of Alameda County Supervisor David Haubert responded but said he would not be available to comment until noon. Oakland Jul 9 Oakland Jul 9 Oakland Jan 15 Oakland Roots one of two finalists for Howard Terminal takeover

headlines.title: SF charter amendments backed by Mayor Lurie qualify for November ballot
headlines.description: Three San Francisco charter amendments backed by Mayor Daniel Lurie have qualified for the November ballot. Lurie announced the measures Wednesday and called on San Franciscans to vote in favor of them. Using the slogan “Clean Up City Hall,” the mayor made the announcement in front of a public restroom in Noe Valley that he said highlights the cost and difficulty of building projects in San Francisco. According to the mayor, the three charter amendments are intended to address areas of the city charter that have contributed to those challenges. NBC Bay Area’s Kris Sanchez has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: Apple to lease devices through new ‘Apple Upgrade' program
headlines.description: Apple is launching a new program that will allow users to lease devices. The program is called “Apple Upgrade,” and customers will be able to lease iPhones for as little as $17.99 per month for up to two years. To make this possible, Apple is partnering with Klarna, the buy now, pay later company. There will be similar lease options for additional devices such as iPads, Apple Watches and MacBooks. Following the two-year lease, customers will have the option to return, buy or trade in the device.

headlines.title: Woman details past affair with Gavin Newsom
headlines.description: The woman California Gov. Gavin Newsom had an affair with 20 years ago shared her story in Vanity Fair magazine. Ruby Rippey worked as Newsom’s appointment secretary when he served as mayor of San Francisco. At the time of the affair, Rippey was married to a top aide to Newsom, Alex Tourk. In a first-person account published in Vanity Fair Tuesday, Rippey discussed her yearslong battle with alcoholism, details of the affair and how it ultimately ended. In 2007, Newsom held a news conference in which he ultimately admitted to the affair. According to her own social media post, Rippey told her side of the story now partially because Newsom mentioned her in his memoir. A spokesperson for Newsom told The New York Times, “The governor acknowledged his role and publicly apologized for his conduct nearly two decades ago when he was still mayor. In the time since, he met his wife, started a family and has focused on serving Californians.” The magazine piece comes as Newsom finishes up his time as California governor and considers plans to run for president of the United States.

headlines.title: New poll reveals concerns of young California voters
headlines.description: Faith that the government will meet their needs is fading among young Californians. That’s according to a new poll presented Wednesday by Power California that points to what could sway this generation of voters in the 2026 midterms. The virtual presentation was led by Saa’un Bell, executive vice president of Power California, a statewide civic engagement organization that works with community partners across the state to build political power among young people of color and push for a government that reflects California’s diversity. Bell was joined by Andrew Proctor, senior analyst at Latino Decisions, the firm that conducted the poll, along with three young voters who spoke to the findings through their own experiences: Christian Caguiat, of Hayward; Jackie Avila, 26, of Fresno; and Adan Primero, 21, of East Los Angeles. The survey polled 1,567 Californians between the ages of 18 and 30 throughout May and June. “Economic survival has replaced economic mobility,” stated Bell. Caguiat moved constantly growing up and lost his family’s home during the 2008 housing crisis. He lost his health insurance about six months ago after prescription costs tripled or quadrupled, he said, and has since gone without his medications rather than cut into rent and food. Caguiat grew up watching his parents skip doctor’s appointments to go to work, which left him wary of seeking medical care himself. He has said the choice often came down to paying for “a roof over his head” or risking debt from a recommended treatment. That trade-off showed up in the poll’s numbers as well: 15% of young Californians said they had postponed medical or dental care in the past year because of the cost of living, and 34% said cuts to Medicaid and Medi-Cal have personally affected them, the second-highest share among the federal policies tested. Avila grew up in Fresno amid periods of financial instability, including a stretch in middle school when her family lived in hotels. She recalled the moment her family finally secured permanent housing by describing lying on the carpet, arms at her sides, in relief. Avila now lives with her mother in low-income housing with her two children and is looking for work as an emergency medical technician. The poll found her home region carrying the heaviest load in the state: 84% of young Central Valley residents reported at least one economic hardship in the past year, the highest rate of any region, and 59% said California is “being built for someone else” rather than for people like them. Despite that strain, the Central Valley posted the highest rates of political engagement in the state, according to the poll. Primero grew up in East Los Angeles as the youngest of six children, with parents who often worked as street vendors. He said that upbringing put him close to the effects of economic downturns and policy decisions early on, from the 2008 recession to immigration raids and other disruptions that made it difficult for people to be outside, restrictions that didn’t just keep his parents from working but kept away the customers whose business sustained the family. His account tracks with one of the poll’s findings, where respondents cite federal policies that have personally affected them: 33% cited immigration detainments and deportations, while 35%, the highest share tested, pointed to cuts to federal services, jobs and funding. Broader results from the poll echoed the pressures described by Primero, Avila and Caguiat. Eighty percent of respondents said the cost of living is outpacing their wages, and 71% reported experiencing at least one concrete hardship in the past year, with young Black Californians reporting the heaviest burden across nearly every measure tested. Cost of living and inflation ranked as the single biggest motivator for the 2026 midterms, followed by opposition to the Trump administration, including among voters registered with no party preference. The poll points to deep skepticism toward institutions broadly. When asked why young people vote at lower rates despite making up a majority of the state’s eligible voters, 40% of respondents pointed to a belief that nothing changes and 40% cited distrust of politicians, while 38% said they are too busy trying to survive. Respondents said they trust parents, friends and local organizations far more than political parties, influencers or faith leaders when forming opinions or deciding how to vote. “Young voters aren’t losing hope, they’re losing patience,” Bell said. Bell closed the briefing by asking Primero, Avila and Caguiat what they want elected officials to understand about their generation, a question Avila’s answer spoke to directly. “We’re real people, despite what we go through, we’re willing to do the work,” Avila said. “And there’s much we want to see changed, but we can’t change if we’re not given the opportunity.”

headlines.title: Woman allegedly sprays bear repellent during argument in Lafayette
headlines.description: A 74-year-old woman was arrested over the weekend after she allegedly used bear spray during an argument in a Trader Joe’s parking lot in Lafayette. Lafayette police were called about 10:40 a.m. Saturday to the store in the 3600 block of Mt. Diablo Boulevard. Witnesses told officers that the woman was arguing with someone and allegedly pointed the bear spray out her driver’s side window and sprayed someone. As the other person drove away, she allegedly sprayed the repellent a second time, police said. The suspect then drove away, but witnesses gave officers her license plate, helping Orinda police spot her car. They pulled her over and detained her on westbound Highway 24. Police didn’t release information about the nature of the argument. Eight people were exposed to the bear spray and were treated at the scene by Contra Costa County Fire Protection District crews. One person was transported to a hospital. The suspect, Oakland resident Monica Thomas, was booked at the Martinez Jail on suspicion of assault with a deadly weapon and unlawful use of tear gas.

headlines.title: Man who allegedly stabbed person at Fremont party charged with attempted murder
headlines.description: A man accused of stabbing someone at a party in Fremont has been charged with attempted murder and other crimes, the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office said Tuesday. Taylor Maxfield Clausen, 37, is charged with attempted murder, assault with a deadly weapon and the personal use of a knife, according to prosecutors. On Saturday, the district attorney’s office alleges that Clausen was at a party and stabbed someone in the neck, injuring them. Clausen is being held without bail and is scheduled to be arraigned on Wednesday in Dublin.

headlines.title: James Beere sworn in as Oakland police chief
headlines.description: James Beere was sworn in as Oakland’s police chief, becoming the city’s seventh chief or interim chief in the past six years. Mayor Barbara Lee swore in Beere Wednesday morning during a ceremony at Oakland City Hall. Beere has been with the Oakland Police Department for 29 years and has served as interim chief since Floyd Mitchell resigned last year. He becomes Oakland’s 12th police chief — permanent or interim — in the past 15 years. Mayor Lee said she expects Beere to bring stability to the department. She said she was looking for someone who understands both policing and Oakland and views the position as a commitment to the city. Oakland Jul 9 Oakland Mar 24 Beere’s appointment comes as the Oakland Police Department is expected to come out from under federal oversight later this year. Beere said he is committed to continuing the policing strategies outlined in the oversight agreement even after federal oversight ends. His priorities include recruiting more officers for the chronically understaffed department, constitutional policing, rebuilding trust and continuing to reduce crime. “We’ve got to keep our foot on the gas,” Beere said. “We’ve got to keep in touch with what’s going on in the community. And we’ve got to keep those lines of communication open.” The Oakland Police Officers’ Association has backed Mayor Lee’s decision to appoint Beere as permanent chief.
